SNPs can be produced in smaller sizes and used to improve the functional properties of starch. Thus, they are considered for the various opportunities to improve the quality of product development with starch. This literature study presents information and reviews regarding SNPs, their general preparation methods, characteristics of the resulting SNPs and their applications, especially in food systems, such as Pickering emulsion, bioplastic filler, antimicrobial agent, fat replacer and encapsulating agent. The aspects related to the properties of SNPs and information on the extent of their utilisation are reviewed in this study. The findings can be utilised and encouraged by other researchers to develop and expand the applications of SNPs. Keywords: starch nanoparticle, preparation, properties, applications 1. Introduction Starch is a native polymer that is abundantly available and widely used worldwide [1,2]. Starch is a carbohydrate. Starch granules are a source of carbohydrates and renewable substances produced by plants in the form of granular constituents of plant parts, such as seeds, tubers and fruits, as sources of stored energy; the shape and nature of starch depend on the botanical source, climate and location from where it is isolated [3,4,5,6,7]. Globally, starch production is mainly based on four raw materials, namely, corn, cassava, wheat and potatoes, with >75% of starch produced from corn [8,9]. Starch is a mixture of two macromolecules, namely amylose with linear chains of glucose molecules connected by α-1,4 glucosidic bonds, and amylopectin with branched chains consisting of short amylose groups connected by α-1,6 glucosidic bonds [10,11]. In general, starch contains about 20–30% amylose and 70–80% amylopectin, depending on the source [12]. The ratio of amylose/amylopectin content will affect the functional properties of starch, such as gelatinisation, viscosity and gel stability [13]. Starch has been widely used as an additive in the food industry and other industrial applications, such as pharmaceuticals, drug delivery and composites, because of its low cost and easy availability [14,15]. In the food industry, it is generally used as a thickener and an auxiliary to improve food texture and can be utilized to manufacture sauces, soups and puddings [16,17]. Native starch directly extracted from plants generally has limited industrial-scale applications. It has low thermal stability and resistance to external factors during storage, high brittleness and a hydrophilic nature [18]. Therefore, additional treatment, either physically, chemically or enzymatically, is needed to change the properties of native starch to overcome its limitations [16,19,20,21,22,23,24,25]. For decades, the food industry has attempted to improve the physicochemical properties of starch to ensure the final quality of food products [26]. Several starch studies have focused on particle size and understanding the relationship between nano- and microscopic properties of different materials, where the resulting particles are small and have a large surface area [16,27]. This new alternative, the modification of starch macromolecules from micro- to nanoscale, produces nanostarches, which have attracted considerable attention due to their unique properties, and not only change the particle size, but also enhances their functional properties [6,26]. Nanostarches are of two types: starch nanocrystals (SNCs) are crystalline portions resulting from the disruption of amorphous domains in starch granules, and starch nanoparticles (SNPs) generated from gelatinised starch, which may include amorphous regions [27,28]. SNPs are considered promising biomaterials and offer various opportunities for quality improvement for the innovative development of competitive products [29,30]. SNPs have been widely used in active food packaging [31], bioactive compound encapsulation [32], nanocomposite film [33] and Pickering emulsion stabilisers [11,34]. This review focuses on SNPs, their various preparation methods, including physical, chemical and enzymatic treatments, and the resulting characteristic changes. Characterisation of SNPs in terms of size distribution, crystal structure and various properties compared with native starch and the extent to which SNPs have been utilised were also reviewed. Furthermore, Le Corre et al. [36] reported that the morphology and properties of the resulting nanoparticles depend on the botanical source. Some previous studies on SNPs, such as those from potatoes [6], bananas [37], water chestnuts [38], sago [39] and maize starches [40], have been widely carried out. In general, the preparation of SNPs can be classified into ‘top-down’ and ‘bottom-up’ methods [41]. On the other hand, top-down methods, such as ultrasonication, homogenisation, gamma radiation, acid hydrolysis and others, involve the production of nanoparticles from the breakdown of large particles into small ones based on structural fragmentation using mechanical and chemical forces [30,42]. On the other hand, bottom-up methods produce nanoparticles using a thermodynamic process of controlled molecular assembly, such as nanoprecipitation or self-assembly [42]. fetched_contents.text: Biodegradability Evaluation of Polymers by ISO 14855-2 Abstract Biodegradabilities of polymers and their composites in a controlled compost were described. Polycaprolactone (PCL) and poly(lactic acid) (PLA) were employed as biodegradable polymers. Biodegradabilities of PCL and PLA samples in a controlled compost were measured using a Microbial Oxidative Degradation Analyzer (MODA) according to ISO 14855-2. Sample preparation method for biodegradation test according to ISO/DIS 10210 was also described. Effects of sizes and shapes of samples on biodegradability were studied. Reproducibility of biodegradation test of ISO 14855-2 by MODA was confirmed. Validity of sample preparation method for polymer pellets, polymer film, and polymer products of ISO/DIS 10210 for ISO 14855-2 was confirmed. Keywords: biodegradability, polycaprolactone, poly(lactic acid), compost, evaluation, ISO 14855-2, ISO/DIS 10210 1. Introduction Polymers are widely used in various industrial fields due to their merits, such as light weight, resistance to chemicals, resistance to the environment, easy processing, etc. It is difficult for polymers to be treated after use due to their resistance to the environment. When polymers are disposed of in a natural environment, they remain for a long time without degradation. One of the solutions to this problem of polymers after use is the development of biodegradable polymers. Biodegradable polymers can be biodegraded eventually by microorganisms in the natural environment into carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O). Various types of biodegradable plastics have been developed. Among these biodegradable plastics, polycaprolactone (PCL) was developed as a biodegradable plastic of the aliphatic polyester type derived from the chemical synthesis of crude petroleum. PCL has good water, oil and chlorine resistance. It has a low melting point (ca. 60 °C), low melt viscosity and it is easy to process. The low melting-point of PCL is expected to be suitable for composting as a means of disposal, since the temperature obtained during composting routinely exceeds 60 °C. PCL is mainly used in thermoplastic polyurethanes, resins for surface coatings, adhesives and synthetic leather and fabrics. It also serves to make stiffeners for shoes and orthopedic splints, and fully biodegradable compostable bags, sutures, and fibers. PCL is often mixed with starch to obtain a good biodegradable material in order to reduce its price. Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) products have become widely used because of their biodegradability, hydrodegradability and the biorenewable profile with its source as vegetables such as corn. This allows both the prevention of environmental pollution and the use of renewable resources for a sustainable society. Starch nanoparticles can alter polymer structure and porosity in ways that may influence biodegradability by creating physical pathways, changing crystallinity and phase behavior, and increasing surface area and porosity. The evidence here is that starch nanoparticles are prepared through methods that fragment or modify starch granules, and that their morphology, size, and porosity can be observed and characterized [N1-F1]. One relevant mechanism is that starch nanoparticles can be produced by breaking down larger particles into smaller ones, and that this process can create nanoporous structures [N1-F1]. The cited evidence also notes that starch granules swell and disintegrate during gelatinization, with amylose chains leaching out and amylopectin crystallites melting, which forms a continuous polymeric network [N1-F1]. This suggests that nanoparticle incorporation can disrupt or modify the native polymer matrix’s packing and continuity, potentially creating physical pathways or voids through which water or microbes can enter [N1-F1].

On nanoparticle dispersion and polymer crystallinity, the evidence indicates that starch nanoparticles are produced by both top-down and bottom-up methods, and that the resulting nanoparticles can have different morphology depending on the botanical source and preparation route [N1-F1]. This implies that nanoparticle dispersion is not uniform and can affect local polymer organization. The cited review also states that starch nanoparticles can be used as nanocomposite fillers and that they can improve functional properties [N1-F1]. While the provided evidence does not explicitly define phase separation in starch nanoparticle-modified polymers, it does support the broader idea that nanoparticle loading can change the physical state of the polymer matrix, including crystallinity and phase behavior [N1-F1].

Regarding nanoparticle size and loading level, the evidence emphasizes that starch nanoparticle size and morphology depend on preparation conditions, and that scanning electron microscopy is used to observe nanoparticle shape, size, and porosity [N1-R3]. It also notes that starch nanoparticles may include amorphous regions and that their properties depend on the source and treatment method [N1-F1]. Since smaller nanoparticles generally increase surface area, and higher loading levels can increase the number of nanoparticle-polymer contacts, the evidence supports the conclusion that nanoparticle size and loading level influence surface area and porosity [N1-F1]. However, the provided evidence does not quantify the exact relationship between loading and porosity, so this remains a contextual inference rather than a direct measurement [N1-F1].

Overall, starch nanoparticles can affect biodegradability by altering the polymer’s physical structure and porosity, which may either expose more surface area for degradation or create pathways that accelerate moisture penetration and microbial access [N1-F1]. The evidence is strongest on morphology, preparation, and surface-area implications, but less direct on specific biodegradation outcomes from those structural changes alone [N1-F1].

Starch nanoparticles and the polymer environment can influence microbial activity by providing nutrients, attachment sites, or enzyme access, while also affecting microbial access and growth through polymer chemistry and nanoparticle shielding. The direct evidence shows that starch-based films are associated with microbial degradation processes, and that starch nanoparticle-containing films can be slower to biodegrade, suggesting that microbial behavior is relevant to biodegradability [N3-R3]. Another study reported that starch nanoparticles prepared by acid hydrolysis containing Ag nanoparticles showed antibacterial activity against *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Salmonella typhi*, indicating that starch nanoparticle systems can support or inhibit microbial growth depending on the added components [N3-R1]. A related review on starch-based films notes that starch films can support microbial degradation because they are biodegradable, and that moisture-induced mechanical degradation can occur alongside microbial action [N2-R1].

On microbes associated with starch and polymer biodegradation, the evidence is broad rather than taxonomically specific. The review on starch-based films describes biodegradable polymers and their microbial degradation in compost, but it does not list a specific microbial community [N2-R1]. The microbial example provided in the nanoparticle evidence refers to *S. aureus* and *S. typhi*, but these are not typical polymer-degrading microbes; instead, they are indicators of antibacterial activity [N3-R1]. Therefore, the strongest microbial evidence here is that starch-based systems are exposed to microbial activity, and that microbial degradation is part of the biodegradation process [N2-R1][N3-R3].

The evidence also indicates that starch nanoparticles can provide attachment sites or substrates for microbes. The review on starch-based films states that starch films can be used in food packaging and that they can support microbial degradation [N2-R1]. In the nanoparticle context, the evidence suggests that starch nanoparticles may be used as filler or functional components that can change the polymer’s surface and structure, potentially creating surfaces that microbes can colonize [N1-F1]. However, the provided evidence does not directly show that starch nanoparticles themselves serve as nutrient sources for microbes, so this remains an inference rather than a direct claim [N1-F1].

Polymer chemistry and nanoparticle shielding are less directly addressed in the cited evidence, but the context is clear. The review on starch-based films explains that starch is hydrophilic and has hydroxyl groups that promote hydrogen bonding, which can limit moisture resistance and dimensional stability [N5-F2]. This implies that polymer chemistry can influence microbial access by affecting water availability and surface properties [N5-F2]. The evidence also shows that starch nanoparticles can be hydrophobically modified, which may shield the polymer surface from moisture and microbes [N6-R2]. Taken together, the evidence supports the idea that polymer chemistry and nanoparticle shielding can either promote microbial access by making surfaces more favorable for microbes or inhibit microbial access by reducing hydrophilicity and surface energy [N5-F2][N6-R2].

Overall, starch nanoparticles can influence microbial activity by altering the polymer environment, providing or blocking attachment sites, and changing the availability of moisture and nutrients. The evidence is strongest on microbial degradation and antibacterial activity, but less precise on the exact microbial identities or the extent of nutrient provision [N2-R1][N3-R1][N3-R3].

The evidence on starch nanoparticles and overall biodegradability is mixed, with some reports suggesting improvement, others indicating reduced biodegradation, and others showing modulation depending on polymer type and test conditions. The most direct biodegradability evidence comes from starch nanoparticle-containing nanocomposites. One study reports that starch nanocomposite films biodegraded slower than neat starch films, with the degradation rate reduced by 46 and 44% in compost and another test environment, respectively [N3-R3]. Another study on starch/poly(lactic acid) nanocomposites found that lactic acid grafted starch nanocrystals affected the rate of soil burial degradation of PLA [N3-R2]. These findings suggest that starch nanoparticles can sometimes reduce biodegradation rate, at least in some polymer systems.

On the other hand, one review states that starch nanoparticles may increase biodegradability by reducing the molecular mass of the packaging polymer, implying that nanoparticle incorporation can improve biodegradation [N1-R2]. This contrasts with the slower-degrading nanocomposite results, showing that the effect depends on the polymer matrix and functionalization. The evidence also notes that starch-based films are inherently biodegradable, which means that biodegradability is not necessarily reduced by all starch nanoparticle additions; rather, it can be altered by how the nanoparticles are integrated into the polymer [N2-R1][N5-F2].

Biodegradation is measured using standard protocols, which is important for interpreting the practical relevance of the findings. The biodegradability evaluation evidence includes ISO 14855-2, which measures biodegradability of polymers and composites in controlled compost using a Microbial Oxidative Degradation Analyzer (MODA) [N4-F3]. It also references ASTM standards such as ASTM 6400 and ASTM D6400, which set thresholds for biodegradation in compost and specify test methods [N4-R2][N4-R4]. These standards are relevant because they define what counts as biodegradation in practice: for example, ASTM D6400 sets a threshold of 60% biodegradation within six months for homopolymers or random copolymers, and 90% for copolymers [N4-R2]. The evidence also mentions ASTM D5988, which uses cellulose or starch as a reference material and requires 70% or more biodegradation within six months [N4-R5]. This shows that biodegradability is measured through standardized microbial tests, and that the results are tied to specific environmental conditions and endpoints [N4-F3][N4-R2][N4-R4].

The conflicting evidence across polymer types and test conditions is clear. For some starch nanoparticle-modified systems, biodegradation is reduced compared to neat starch or unmodified polymer controls [N3-R3]. For other cases, starch nanoparticles may be associated with improved biodegradability because they lower molecular mass or enhance functional properties [N1-R2]. The evidence also shows that moisture-induced mechanical degradation can occur alongside microbial action [N2-R1], meaning that the observed biodegradation outcome may depend on the environment rather than the nanoparticle itself. The biodegradation evaluation evidence further shows that sample preparation method, test environment, and polymer form affect biodegradability results [N4-F3]. This means that starch nanoparticles can modulate biodegradability, but the direction of the effect is polymer-specific and test-condition-dependent [N1-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-F3].

Overall, the evidence suggests that starch nanoparticles may improve, reduce, or modulate biodegradability depending on the polymer matrix, nanoparticle functionalization, and test conditions. The strongest conclusion is that biodegradability is not a single universal effect, and that standardized measurement protocols such as ISO 14855-2 and ASTM D6400 are essential for comparing results [N4-F3][N4-R2]. The evidence is strongest on reported degradation rates and measurement standards, but less precise on the exact mechanisms underlying the differences across polymer types [N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-F3].

This suggests that nanoparticle incorporation can disrupt the native polymer matrix and create new voids or pathways through which water and microbes can enter.

Starch nanoparticles can change moisture content by altering water uptake, swelling, and hydrophilicity. The hydrophobicity review explains that starch-based films are hydrophilic because of their hydroxyl-rich structure, which promotes hydrogen bonding and water interaction, and that hydrophilic surfaces tend to attract water, increasing moisture sensitivity and water vapor permeability [N5-F2]. This means that starch nanoparticle-modified polymers can retain or release moisture differently from native starch.

Moisture interacts with polymer chains to initiate degradation. At the same time, moisture gradients can create localized degradation and crack propagation.
